To visualize the Kuramoto model, picture each phase $\theta_j$ as a point $e^{i\theta_j}$ running around the unit circle in the complex plane [@strogatz2000kuramoto].

```{python}
#| label: fig-kuramoto-circle
#| fig-cap: 'Oscillators (blue dots) on the unit circle. The order parameter (red) points towards the centroid of the phases.'
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from amlab.odes_coupled.kuramoto import initialize_oscillators, kuramoto_order_parameter

num_oscillators = 100
theta, omega = initialize_oscillators(
    num_oscillators,
    distribution="normal",
    scale_omega=0.5,
    scale_phase=0.6,
    seed=1)

x = np.cos(theta)
y = np.sin(theta)

r, phi, rcosphi, rsinphi = kuramoto_order_parameter(theta)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\cos\theta$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\sin\theta$")
ax.set_xlim(-1.1, 1.1)
ax.set_ylim(-1.1, 1.1)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.grid(True)
circle = plt.Circle((0, 0), 1, color="lightgray", fill=False)
ax.add_artist(circle)
ax.scatter(x, y, s=50, color="blue", alpha=0.5)
ax.plot([0, rcosphi], [0, rsinphi], color="red", linewidth=2)
ax.plot([rcosphi], [rsinphi], "ro", markersize=6)
plt.show()
```

## Definition

The complex **order parameter** is the centroid of these points:

$$
r e^{i\psi} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^N e^{i\theta_j}.
$$ {#eq-r-exp}

- $r \in [0, 1]$ is the **coherence**. $r = 1$ when all phases coincide. $r \approx 0$ when the phases are spread around the circle.
- $\psi$ is the **mean phase**, the phase of the collective rhythm.

In @fig-kuramoto-circle the initial phases cover only part of the circle, so the red vector has a clear length and direction. To see the vector move as the phases evolve, run the script [amlab/odes_coupled/kuramoto.py](../../amlab/odes_coupled/kuramoto.py). You build the same animation yourself in [Animation](kuramoto-animation.qmd).

## Mean-field form

Multiply @eq-r-exp by $e^{-i\theta_i}$ and take the imaginary part:

$$
r\sin(\psi - \theta_i) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i).
$$

The Kuramoto model therefore becomes

$$
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + K r \sin(\psi - \theta_i),\quad i = 1, \dots, N.
$$ {#eq-ode-mean-field}

This rewriting is exact for every $N$ [@strogatz2000kuramoto]. Each oscillator no longer sees the others one by one. It sees only the mean field: it is pulled toward the mean phase $\psi$ with effective strength $Kr$. Computing $r$ and $\psi$ costs $O(N)$ operations per step, while the double sum in the pairwise form costs $O(N^2)$.

## Feedback between coherence and coupling

@eq-ode-mean-field shows why synchronization can appear spontaneously [@strogatz2000kuramoto]:

- Oscillators are pulled toward $\psi$ with strength $Kr$.
- If more of them cluster, $r$ grows.
- A larger $r$ increases the pull $Kr$, which recruits more oscillators.

The loop is opposed by the spread of natural frequencies. Oscillators whose $|\omega_i|$ exceeds $Kr$ cannot follow the mean field and keep drifting. The balance sets a threshold coupling $K_c$, derived in [Critical Coupling](critical-coupling.qmd).

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise

Suppose the $N$ phases are independent and uniform on $[0, 2\pi)$. Show that $\mathbb{E}[r^2] = 1/N$. What does this imply for the value of $r$ you measure in an incoherent simulation?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

$$
r^2 = \left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_j e^{i\theta_j}\right|^2 = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{j,k} e^{i(\theta_j - \theta_k)}.
$$

The $N$ terms with $j = k$ equal $1$. For $j \ne k$ the phases are independent, so $\mathbb{E}[e^{i(\theta_j-\theta_k)}] = \mathbb{E}[e^{i\theta_j}]\,\mathbb{E}[e^{-i\theta_k}] = 0$. Hence $\mathbb{E}[r^2] = N/N^2 = 1/N$. An incoherent population with $N = 100$ shows $r$ of order $0.1$, not $0$. You will see this floor in [Finite-Size Effects](kuramoto-finite-size.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise

Compute $r$ for three oscillators at phases $0$, $2\pi/3$ and $4\pi/3$, and for three oscillators at $0$, $0$ and $\pi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

The first three points are the cube roots of unity, which sum to zero, so $r = 0$. For the second set, $e^{0} + e^{0} + e^{i\pi} = 1$, so $r = 1/3$ and $\psi = 0$.
:::
